content: Herpes labialis, also referred to as orolabial herpes, is an infection of the lips caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV). This condition often results in the formation of small blisters or sores around the mouth, commonly known as cold sores or fever blisters. It is important to note that the term herpes labialis specifically refers to the lips and does not pertain to the genital labia, despite the shared etymology of the term labia. When the infection involves both the face and the mouth, it is referred to as orofacial herpes. If the infection is confined to the mouth, it is termed herpetic stomatitis, derived from the Greek word stoma, meaning mouth. The sores caused by herpes labialis typically resolve within two to three weeks. However, the herpes simplex virus remains in the body even after the sores heal. Following the initial infection, the virus becomes dormant in the facial nerves and may periodically reactivate, causing recurrent sores in the same area of the mouth or face as the original infection. Herpes labialis occurs when the herpes simplex virus comes into contact with the oral mucosa or abraded skin around the mouth. The most common causative agent is herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), although cases of oral infection caused by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) are becoming more frequent. Herpes infections are often asymptomatic, but when symptoms do occur, they typically resolve within two weeks. The primary symptom of oral herpes is inflammation of the mucosa of the cheeks and gums, a condition known as acute herpetic gingivostomatitis. This inflammation usually develops within five to ten days of the initial infection. Other symptoms may include painful ulcers, which are sometimes mistaken for canker sores, as well as fever and sore throat. In adolescents, primary HSV infection often presents as severe pharyngitis, with lesions forming on the cheeks and gums. Some individuals may experience difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and swollen lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy). In adults, primary HSV infections may also cause pharyngitis, resembling the symptoms of infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever), although gingivostomatitis is less common in this age group. Recurrent oral infections are more frequently associated with HSV-1 than HSV-2. Before a recurrence, individuals often experience prodromal symptoms such as tingling, itching, or redness around the affected area. This is followed by the development of fluid-filled blisters on the lip tissue and the vermilion border (the area between the lip and the surrounding skin). Recurrent infections are commonly referred to as herpes simplex labialis. Rarely, reinfections may occur inside the mouth, affecting areas such as the gums, alveolar ridge, hard palate, and the back of the tongue. These intraoral infections may occur alongside herpes labialis. Treatment for herpes labialis includes several symptomatic and antiviral approaches. Applying a cool, wet towel or ice to the sore can provide relief. Over-the-counter pain relievers such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or acetaminophen (Tylenol) can help manage discomfort. For severe pain, topical anesthetics like benzocaine (Anbesol, Orajel) in concentrations of 7.5%, 10%, or 20% may be used. Patients experiencing significant pain may find it difficult to consume solid foods; in such cases, maintaining hydration and consuming nutrient-rich smoothies with added protein powder is recommended. Vitamin supplementation may also be beneficial. It is advisable to avoid citrus foods, such as tomatoes and lemons, as they can exacerbate the pain associated with blisters. The application of zinc oxide cream to the cold sore may help reduce the duration of the blister. Antiviral treatments, such as oral acyclovir or over-the-counter docosanol cream (Abreva, 10% formulation), can also shorten the duration of symptoms. For primary lesions, oral acyclovir or topical docosanol applied five times daily has been shown to be effective. An antiviral regimen for herpes labialis may include oral acyclovir at a dose of 15 mg/kg every five hours for seven days.
